events.label: Major Midwest drought: index falls to -4.8
Drought index -7.8, near the 1934 Dust Bowl record

explanation.summary: Does drought make groceries more expensive? The first card shows the national drought index: below zero is dry, and -4 or less is extreme drought. The second shows how much grocery prices rose from a year before. The stripes show every month since 2000: red means drier, or groceries rising faster than the usual 2% a year. The link is weak. The worst grocery inflation, in 2022, came from energy, wages and the war in Ukraine, not drought. The deep drought of 2026 has barely moved grocery prices.
explanation.methodology: Palmer Drought Severity Index for the contiguous US from NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information (Climate at a Glance). Below zero means drier than normal; below -4 is extreme drought. Grocery inflation is the year-over-year change in the BLS CPI for food at home (CUUR0000SAF11).

key_findings.title: July 2012: Corn Belt Drought
key_findings.description: The national drought index fell to -4.8, extreme drought. Grocery inflation stayed low, near 2%, because one bad harvest is a small part of what a grocery bill pays for.
key_findings.significance: Severe drought does not always show up at the supermarket.

key_findings.title: August 2022: Grocery Inflation Peaks at 13.5%
key_findings.description: Food-at-home prices rose 13.5% in a year, the highest on the chart. Drought was moderate (about -2.8); the main causes were energy, transport and labor costs.
key_findings.significance: The biggest grocery shock in 40 years was not caused by weather.

key_findings.title: 2026: Deepest Drought on the Chart
key_findings.description: As of March 2026 the national index reached -7.8, close to the all-time record of -8.4 set in the Dust Bowl (August 1934). Grocery inflation is about 2%.
key_findings.significance: Watch whether this drought reaches food prices with a delay.
